title: Haridasa, teacher of the name
hook: a grandmother born to it and a student who heard a drum, at the same feast. who belongs?
carry: for devotees, bhakti, not birth, opens the door
tomorrow: someone shouts at the singers. why does no one shout back?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Hare Krishnas got their real name, ISKCON, and their aim: Krishna consciousness, keeping Krishna in mind through every task. Today, who gets to belong.

Every group chat has its originals and the people who got added later. A Sunday feast at a Krishna temple can look like that. In the same room: a grandmother whose family prayed to Krishna long before she was born, and a student who first heard his name from a drum on a sidewalk. They chant the same words, off the same page. Can the second one belong the way the first does? Hindus answer that in more than one way.
screen: `THE ORIGINALS AND THE ADDED LATER.` → `A GRANDMOTHER AND A STUDENT.` → `CAN BOTH BELONG?`

segments.voice: The first answer says belonging comes with a family. Being Hindu, on this view, isn't a card you sign. It's a household: a language, a family's gods, festivals kept for generations, ceremonies learned at someone's elbow. Those who hold it are right that a tradition is more than a belief. The second answer is the one these devotees give, and they tell it with a story. In Chaitanya's time lived a man named Haridasa, born into a Muslim family. He fell in love with Krishna's name and chanted it day and night, three hundred thousand names a day, the old account of Chaitanya's life says. In Puri he would not enter the great Jagannath temple; he didn't want to trouble the priests. So he lived in a small hut nearby, and Chaitanya came to him instead, every day. When Haridasa died, Chaitanya carried his body to the sea, sang the names over it, and buried him with his own hands. Devotees still call him Namacharya, the teacher of the name. Behind the story stands a Gita verse. Krishna says, in paraphrase: I am the same to all beings; none is hateful to me, none dear. But those who worship me with devotion are in me, and I in them. For this lineage, that's the open door: bhakti, devotion, not birth. Hindu communities still talk this over, and Haridasa's story holds both sides: a temple door he would not walk through, and a saint who walked out to him.
screen: `BELONGING COMES WITH A FAMILY.` · `HARIDASA: BORN MUSLIM, LIVED ON THE NAME.` · `THE SAINT CAME TO HIS HUT.` · `THE SAME TO ALL BEINGS.` · then, large: `DEVOTION IS THE DOORWAY.`

segments.voice: Haridasa's practice was the name itself. If you'd like, say a name of God softly ten times, Krishna, Rama, or the name you grew up with, slowly, counting on your fingers the way devotees count on beads. If you don't pray, write the name of someone who made room for you when you were the new face, and breathe with them in mind.
The Hare Krishnas: a movement whose door, devotees say, opens on devotion rather than birth.
Your line from Haridasa's hut: for these devotees, bhakti, not birth, opens the door. Until tomorrow.

ISKCON.meaning: International Society for Krishna Consciousness, the Hare Krishnas' own name

Haridasa.meaning: a devotee of Krishna's name in Chaitanya's circle, born into a Muslim family

Namacharya.meaning: teacher of the name, the title devotees give Haridasa

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 9.29 (I am the same to all beings; none is hateful, none dear; those who worship me with devotion are in me, and I in them)
